newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA SHOULD SEEK DEBT FORGIVENESS-U.S. ADVISER.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA SHOULD SEEK DEBT FORGIVENESS-U.S. ADVISER.

text.p: A U.S. economist advising the Bulgarian president said on Monday the crisis-torn Balkan country should seek ways to restructure its heavy debt burden both in the short and long term.

"A country in a hyper-inflationary process can not be expected to make net payments to the outside world to any significant extent. It is just not possible," economist Jeffrey Sachs told a news conference.

He urged the goverment to "find a package which is satisfactory for the creditor and for the country" suggesting postponing payments, finding new loans to pay old loans and seeking long-term solutions.

Sachs, director of the Harvard Institute of Development, has helped governments such as Russia and Poland get on the road to economic reform, visited Bulgaria for four days to advise President Petar Stoyanov on stabilising the economy.
This year alone Bulgaria faces $1 billion foreign payments on its $10 billion debt to governments, commercial creditors and international lending institutions.

"It is possible to reduce very sharply the amount that Bulgaria will actually pay this year under agreements with various creditors. Each one needs to be handled separately, because they have different legal and financial characteristics," he said.
The size of the debt almost equals the country's gross domestic product (GDP) and this year's payments amount to around 10 percent of GDP, which fell last year by nine percent, said Sachs.
"It is clear that if there are no resolutions to these deep problems, to continue payment of all the debts becomes problematic," said Sachs.

Bulgaria's interim cabinet, in power until after general elections on April 19, is seeking to roll over up to $50 million due from part of the non-rescheduled payments due to the Paris Club of official creditors.
Under three agreements rescheduling a $1.2 billion debt owed to the Paris club by 1995, Bulgaria is due to pay official creditors $126 million this year.

"The Paris Club should look into this quite seriously. The issue right now is to roll over substantially the net amounts that must be paid. But in the future one is going to have to look for more creative long-term solutions," said Sachs.

His visit coincided with an International Monetary Fund mission in Bulgaria to negotiate a new funding agreement aimed to help the country stabilise its crumbling currency and banking system and repay foreign debts. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
